flawed_step: Dropping the bridgeless hypothesis permits several bridges incident to one vertex; parity can force every such bridge into a perfect matching, which is impossible.
counterexample: Let the vertices be c and, for each i=1,2,3, five vertices a_i,b_i,d_i,e_i,x_i. For each i, add edges x_i-a_i, x_i-b_i, a_i-d_i, a_i-e_i, b_i-d_i, b_i-e_i, d_i-e_i, and c-x_i. This is a finite simple connected 3-regular graph. Each set L_i={a_i,b_i,d_i,e_i,x_i} has five vertices and c-x_i is its only edge to the rest of the graph. Any perfect matching must therefore contain c-x_i: otherwise all five vertices of L_i would have to be paired internally, which is impossible. Thus a perfect matching would have to contain all three edges c-x_1,c-x_2,c-x_3, contradicting that c can be covered exactly once.
assessment_summary: The explicit 16-vertex connected cubic graph above has no perfect matching, so the bridgeless hypothesis cannot be dropped.
